pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–7; know that indigenous peoples such as the Yanomami have lived in rainforests for thousands of years, building homes from forest materials, finding food by hunting, fishing and gathering, and knowing the forest deeply.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Geography (understand human geography including where people live; use basic geographical vocabulary) and KS1 Science 'Animals, including humans' (humans meet needs from their environment); links to KS1 History/citizenship respect-for-others themes.
• Standards — US: NGSS K-ESS3-1 (humans and where they live) flavour; social-studies strand on how communities meet needs from local resources.
• Operational details — present indigenous peoples as living, CONTEMPORARY communities (present tense: 'the Yanomami live in the Amazon today'), NOT a costume or a museum relic. Anchor to material culture the child can see: a communal shabono home made from forest wood and leaves, gathering fruit, fishing a river, using plants for medicine. Foreground RESPECT for their deep forest knowledge. Use correct people-names; avoid generic 'tribe' framing and any 'primitive' language.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (5): name one thing the Yanomami get from the rainforest (home, food or medicine). Tier B (6): explain that indigenous peoples have lived in the rainforest for a very long time and know it very well. Tier C (7): describe two ways the forest provides for them (e.g. shelter and food) and why their knowledge matters.
bestPractices: Use the present tense and correct people-names (Yanomami) — these are living communities today, not a story from the past.
Anchor learning in material culture the child can see (shabono home, fishing, gathered fruit, medicine plants) rather than abstract claims.
Foreground respect: the forest knowledge these communities hold is deep and valuable, something to admire.
Avoid 'primitive/simple' framing and generic 'tribe' language; sidestep spectacle or costume framing.
Link each aspect of life to the forest as provider (home, food, medicine), reinforcing the rainforest-as-habitat idea.
keyRepresentations: A curated scene of a Yanomami shabono (communal round home) in its forest setting.
Forest→need pairing cards: wood/leaves→home, river/fruit→food, plant→medicine.
A 'long time' timeline cue — 'thousands of years' shown simply for young children.
A map dot in the Amazon showing where the Yanomami live today.
commonMisconceptions: 'Indigenous peoples lived long ago / don't exist any more' — in fact the Yanomami and many others live in rainforests today.
'They are primitive or don't know much' — the opposite: they hold extremely deep, expert knowledge of the forest.
'Everyone lives in houses and shops like mine' — not realising people can meet all their needs directly from the forest.
'It's a costume/dressing-up thing' — treating a living culture as a fancy-dress theme rather than real people's lives.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: understand that indigenous peoples such as the Yanomami are living communities in the Amazon today who have lived in the rainforest for thousands of years, building homes from forest materials, finding food by hunting, fishing and gathering, and holding deep, expert knowledge of the forest's plants and animals. Teaching uses present tense, correct people-names, and foregrounds respect — avoiding 'primitive', generic 'tribe', and costume/spectacle framing. Core activities anchor each part of life (home, food, medicine) to the forest as provider; a respectful first-person meeting and a dignified matching check are offered as alternatives with distinct purposes rather than ranked as superior.

activities.title: Explore a Yanomami home scene: where does everything come from?
feedback: When a learner pairs a forest resource to a need, confirm the link in plain words: 'Yes — the roof is made from forest wood and palm leaves.'
If a learner speaks of the Yanomami only in the past tense, gently restate in the present: 'They live in the Amazon today, right now.'
If a learner treats the knowledge as simple or lucky, add: 'They have learned which plants to use as medicine over many, many generations — that is deep, expert knowledge.'
Reinforce using the correct name rather than generic labels: 'We call them by their own name, the Yanomami.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring abstract ideas (a very long history; deep knowledge) to concrete material culture a child can see — shabono, river fishing, gathered fruit, medicine plant — plus a map location makes the forest-as-provider and living-community links tangible, while present tense and correct names counter the 'they lived long ago / are primitive' misconceptions. A fixed, curated picture can be reviewed for cultural accuracy and dignity and still support this exploration; tap-to-reveal flaps are one optional way to stage each forest→need link.
sourceClaims: The Yanomami are a contemporary indigenous people of the Amazon rainforest (Brazil/Venezuela) who live in communal shabono dwellings and subsist by hunting, fishing, gathering and gardening
KS1 geography teaches where and how people live and the use of local resources; teaching about indigenous peoples should present them as living contemporary communities
learnerActions: Look at a warm, accurate picture of Yanomami life in the Amazon today, centred on a great circular shabono (communal round home) in its forest setting.
Find the Yanomami on a simple map of the Amazon, noting this is a real place where they live today.
Point to the curved roof and answer the question 'What is this home made from?' — then reveal it is built from forest wood and woven palm leaves, by people who know exactly which trees to use.
Point to the river and describe what the family is doing (fishing), point to someone setting off to hunt in the forest, then point to a basket and find gathered fruits and nuts.
Point to a leafy plant and learn it is used as medicine, with knowledge of forest medicines passed down over many generations.
Say out loud, for each thing you found, which need it meets — home, food or medicine — and that it comes from the forest.
Practise using the people's own name: 'the Yanomami live in the Amazon today.'
activities.intendedInsight: Many things the Yanomami need — materials for their homes, food and medicine — come from the forest they understand so deeply, and these are real people living in the world right now whose knowledge deserves respect, not a story from long ago.

activities.title: Meet someone who lives in the rainforest
feedback: Affirm questions that show curiosity about knowledge and daily life; redirect any question that treats the person as 'odd' toward respectful wording.
If the child frames the exchange as about the past, bring it back to the present: 'This is how they live now.'
Praise listening-and-retelling: 'You listened well — tell me the one thing you learned.'
activities.rationale: A first-person, responsive exchange can humanise the topic and may surface the source of deep forest knowledge through dialogue. It is offered as an alternative with a different affordance (a child can ask and hear a reply), and it carries real authenticity/representation risks that a curated image largely avoids; neither medium is inherently superior, and any such portrayal should be co-designed with community voices.
sourceClaims: The Yanomami are a contemporary indigenous people of the Amazon rainforest (Brazil/Venezuela) who live in communal shabono dwellings and subsist by hunting, fishing, gathering and gardening
learnerActions: Have a warm, respectful spoken exchange with a (sensitively, in-role) Yanomami child or elder about daily life: where they sleep, what they eat, how they find medicine.
Ask one question of your own, such as 'How did you learn which plants help when someone is sick?'
Listen to the reply and say back one thing you learned about how the forest provides for them.
Talk about why it would be rude to treat their way of living as 'strange' or as dressing-up, and what is admirable about their forest knowledge.
activities.intendedInsight: Indigenous peoples are real people living today with daily lives and expert knowledge learned over many generations — a person to meet and admire, not an exotic spectacle.

activities.title: Match the need to what the forest provides
feedback: Confirm correct matches with the reason: 'Right — the river gives fish, which is food.'
If a learner reduces the matching to a game of 'being' someone, redirect to matching resources to needs with dignity.
Prompt the respect dimension if missing: 'Who knows which plant is the medicine? People who have learned the forest over many generations.'
activities.rationale: A dignified matching task reinforces the forest-as-provider links and can serve as a light check of the evidence points. A sort or match can check that a child classifies resources to needs, but does not by itself elicit the respect or reasoning at the heart of the topic; framing matters — keep it about resources and needs, not 'playing' at being a person, so it does not trivialise a living culture.
sourceClaims: The Yanomami are a contemporary indigenous people of the Amazon rainforest (Brazil/Venezuela) who live in communal shabono dwellings and subsist by hunting, fishing, gathering and gardening
learnerActions: Sort or match cards: place 'home' with wood and woven palm leaves; place 'food' with the river (fish) and the basket (fruit and nuts); place 'medicine' with the leafy plant.
For each match, say the forest→need link aloud: 'The forest gives wood and leaves, so they can build a home.'
Add, where you can, that they have known these plants and places for a very long time — thousands of years.
activities.intendedInsight: Each basic need — shelter, food, medicine — can be met from the rainforest the Yanomami know well.

constraints: Always use the present tense and the people's own name (Yanomami): these are living communities today, not a story from the past or a costume theme.
Avoid 'primitive', 'simple', 'backward' framing and generic 'tribe' language; sidestep spectacle, dressing-up or 'exotic other' framing.
Foreground respect: present the forest knowledge as deep, expert and admirable, built over many generations.

Any first-person/in-role portrayal should be co-designed with community voices and kept as a warm 'meet someone who lives here' exchange, never an interrogation of an 'exotic' other; it carries authenticity and representation risks.

A matching or multiple-choice check can verify recall and classification of forest→need links but does not by itself elicit the respect or reasoning at the heart of the topic; use it as a light companion, not the main task.

A curated picture is a fixed scene the child cannot alter and cannot respond to a child's own questions; it supports looking, naming and reasoning. A responsive conversation offers a different affordance (asking and hearing a reply) but carries authenticity/representation risks — neither medium is inherently superior for this topic.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 5) name one thing the Yanomami get from the rainforest (home, food or medicine); Tier B (age 6) explain that indigenous peoples have lived in the rainforest for a very long time and know it very well; Tier C (age 7) describe two ways the forest provides (e.g. shelter and food) and why their knowledge matters.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both source claims are marked verified:false in the original row; the contemporary-community and subsistence details rest on unverified sources and should be checked against current, community-authored material before use.

The original 3D 'walk through their village' option was rated poorest partly on ethical grounds (risk of staging a living community as a diorama). That ethical concern is genuine; the comparative claim that 3D 'adds nothing' is a catalog preference and is not asserted here as a universal law.

The row's two-tier diagnostic prompt and probe-deeper questions (including the reason-tier 'why they know the forest so well') are reflected implicitly in the scene feedback and the 'meet someone' dialogue, but are not rendered as discrete learner-facing items; if used directly they would need to be added and cultural-sensitivity reviewed.

The 'meet someone who lives here' activity voices a living indigenous person in persona; this remains an unresolved design/ethics question and is included only with explicit authenticity caveats, not as an endorsed interaction.

probeDeeper: Name one way rainforest peoples use the forest in their daily life.
How do you think they learned so much about the forest's plants and animals?
Why is it important to call peoples by their own names, like the Yanomami?
assess.correctAnswer: They are real people living today (not just from long ago). Peoples like the Yanomami have lived in the rainforest for thousands of years and still do, and they know it deeply because they use its plants, animals and materials every day for food, shelter and medicine — knowledge passed down over many generations.

errorPatterns.pattern: indigenous peoples lived long ago / are 'primitive' — 'they're from history, not now'
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the present tense; they are living communities and expert forest scientists in their own right
errorPatterns.distractor: They only lived long ago and don't exist any more
errorPatterns.revealedBy: talks about them only in the past tense or as backward

errorPatterns.pattern: they don't really know much / just 'survive' — undervalues their ecological expertise
errorPatterns.nextMove: highlight detailed plant/medicine/animal knowledge built over generations that scientists are still learning from
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats their knowledge as luck or basic survival

responseLevels.gap: Speaks of indigenous peoples only as past or 'primitive'; no sense of living expertise.
responseLevels.full: Describes indigenous peoples as living communities today with deep, generations-old knowledge of the forest's plants, animals and materials, and shows respect by using their names and the present tense.
responseLevels.partial: Knows people live in the rainforest and use it, but slips into the past tense or undervalues their knowledge.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Do indigenous rainforest peoples like the Yanomami only exist in stories from long ago, or are they real people living today? Tell me which, and then tell me WHY they know the forest so well.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks indigenous peoples are 'from the past' or 'primitive' holds the documented misconception; the concept child knows they are living contemporary peoples with deep expert knowledge. The reason-tier surfaces the source of that knowledge (living with and using the forest).
